title: Restorative procedures: fillings
blurb: Black's cavity classes, matrix bands and wedges, amalgam and composite trays, the bonding sequence and what to do when things go wrong.
question: The dentist has prepared a cavity on the mesial and occlusal surfaces of 46 and asks for a matrix, a wedge and then 'etch, please'. What class of cavity is this, why is the matrix and wedge needed, and what sequence follows the etch?

teach.body: When decay or a fracture is removed, the dentist shapes a cavity and fills it with a restorative material, most often amalgam or composite (glass ionomer is used too). Your job is to lay out the right tray, keep the tooth dry, prepare and pass materials at the right moment, operate the curing light, aspirate, and spot problems early. Knowing the cavity class tells you what to prepare: a proximal cavity means a matrix band and wedge.

head: Class
Where
Example
rows: Proximal surface of a premolar or molar
Proximal surface of an incisor or canine
Proximal of an incisor or canine, incisal angle lost
Cervical third (near the gum), buccal/labial or lingual/palatal
teach.caption: Class I also includes buccal pits of molars and the palatal pits of upper incisors.

teach.h: Class II and Class IV on the chart
teach.caption: Charted as you face the patient: both teeth are on the patient's right, so mesial is on the right. A Class III cavity on 11 would be M only. Once the incisal corner is involved (MI), it becomes Class IV.

teach.body: A Class II cavity has lost a side wall, so there is nothing to pack material against. A matrix band wraps round the tooth to replace the missing wall, give the filling its shape and create a contact point with the next tooth. A wedge (wooden or plastic) goes in the gap between the teeth at the gum margin to press the band tightly against the tooth, preventing an overhang (a plaque trap). Composite often uses sectional matrices with a ring; front teeth use clear strips.

root.label: A wall is missing
root.sub: Matrix plus a wedge at the gum

teach.caption: The wedge presses the band tight against the tooth at the gum margin, so no overhang (plaque trap) forms. A sectional matrix and ring help composite make a tight contact.
Both trays: mirror, probe, tweezers, excavators, handpieces and burs, matrix and wedges, articulating paper, cotton rolls, suction.

teach.body: Amalgam is held in by the shape of the cavity, not by bonding. It is condensed in small increments to squeeze out voids and adapt it to the cavity walls. Under a deep amalgam a lining is placed, because metal conducts heat and cold to the pulp. Mercury hygiene matters: use capsules, never touch it, and put waste in the amalgam container with mercury suppressant. Under the EU Mercury Regulation (kept in GB law), since July 2018 amalgam should not be used for baby teeth, under-15s or pregnant or breastfeeding patients unless the dentist judges it strictly necessary.

steps.label: Etch
steps.sub: Phosphoric acid gel for the set time

steps.label: Rinse
steps.sub: Wash off etch and dissolved mineral

steps.label: Bond, then cure
steps.sub: Apply bonding agent and light-cure it

teach.caption: Small increments reduce shrinkage stress and let the light cure each layer fully. Shield everyone's eyes from the curing light with an orange filter.

head: Problem
What to do
rows: Composite soft or tacky after curing
Inadequate cure: tell operator, check the light
Wrong powder:liquid ratio or dirty pad
Discard and remix on a clean surface
Syringe tip touched a non-sterile surface
Band lifts or springs when tightened
Patient says the filling feels high
Operator checks the bite before they leave

teach.text: Class III vs Class IV: both are on the proximal surface of a FRONT tooth. Class IV includes the incisal angle (the corner). And don't remove a matrix band before the material has set: the filling can fracture or lose its contour.

items: Black's: I pits and fissures, II proximal back teeth, III proximal front teeth, IV plus incisal angle, V cervical.
Matrix band replaces the missing wall; wedge adapts it at the gum margin and prevents overhangs.
Amalgam: condensed in increments; lining under deep cavities; mercury hygiene.
Composite: etch, rinse, controlled dry, bond, cure, increments each cured, finish, check bite.
Spot and report problems: soft composite, contamination, wrong mix, high filling.

summary: You can now classify any cavity using Black's classification, explain why a matrix band and wedge are used, lay out amalgam and composite trays, follow the composite bonding sequence step by step, and respond correctly when a mix, cure or matrix goes wrong.

A.q: The dentist prepares a cavity involving the distal and occlusal surfaces of 25. What is its Black's class?
options: Class I
Class II
Class III
Class V
A.why: Class II cavities involve a proximal (mesial or distal) surface of a premolar or molar. 25 is a premolar, so DO is Class II.

whyNot.0: Class I involves pits and fissures only, not a proximal surface.
whyNot.2: Class III is a proximal cavity on an incisor or canine.
whyNot.3: Class V is at the cervical third of a buccal or lingual surface.

A.q: A cavity has been prepared for a direct composite. Which sequence comes next?
options: Bond, etch, cure, rinse, place composite
Rinse, bond, etch, dry, place composite
Place composite, etch, rinse, bond, cure
Etch, rinse, dry, bond, cure, composite
A.why: Etch roughens the tooth, rinsing removes it, controlled drying prepares the surface, then bond is applied and cured before composite goes in.

whyNot.0: Bond goes on after etching and rinsing, not before.
whyNot.1: Bonding before etching would prevent the etch from working.
whyNot.2: Composite needs a bonded surface first, so it comes last.

A.q: A wooden wedge is placed between the teeth before a Class II filling is packed. What is its main purpose?
options: To hold the rubber dam sheet in place
To keep the patient's mouth wide open
To adapt the band at the gum margin
To protect the pulp from the heat
A.why: The wedge presses the matrix band against the tooth at the gingival margin, preventing an overhang of filling material.

whyNot.0: Rubber dam is held by a clamp and frame.
whyNot.1: A mouth prop keeps the mouth open, not a wedge.
whyNot.3: A lining protects the pulp; the wedge works at the gum margin.

B.q: A patient has chipped the corner off an upper central incisor, including the incisal angle. What class is the cavity?
options: Class II
Class III
Class V
Class IV
B.why: Class IV is a proximal cavity on an incisor or canine that includes the incisal angle.

whyNot.0: Class II is on premolars and molars.
whyNot.1: Class III is proximal on a front tooth but does NOT include the incisal angle.
whyNot.2: Class V is at the cervical third, near the gum.

B.q: A posterior composite is still soft and tacky after the normal curing time. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The composite was cured too long
It was not cured adequately
Too much etch was applied
The matrix band was too tight
B.why: Soft, tacky composite after curing suggests inadequate curing: the light may be faulty, dirty, held too far away or used too briefly, or the layer too thick.

whyNot.2: Excess etch affects bonding, not how hard the composite sets.
whyNot.3: Band tightness doesn't stop composite curing.

B.q: Why is amalgam condensed in small increments rather than packed in one go?
options: To remove voids and adapt it to the walls
To speed up the setting reaction in the mouth
To make the filling tooth-coloured
To bond it chemically to the dentine
B.why: Condensing small increments squeezes out air and excess mercury and pushes the alloy against every wall, giving a dense, well-adapted filling.

whyNot.2: Amalgam is silver-grey whatever the technique.
whyNot.3: Amalgam doesn't bond chemically; it is held by cavity shape.

C.q: A cavity is at the neck of 34 on the buccal surface, near the gum. What is its Black's class?
options: Class V
Class I
Class II
Class III
C.why: Class V cavities are in the cervical third (gingival third) of the buccal/labial or lingual/palatal surface of any tooth.

whyNot.1: Class I involves pits and fissures.
whyNot.2: Class II involves a proximal surface of a back tooth.
whyNot.3: Class III is proximal on a front tooth.

C.q: As the retainer is tightened, the matrix band keeps springing away from the gingival margin. What is the most likely reason?
options: The amalgam capsule was mixed far too wet
The band is poorly seated or assembled
The curing light is not working
The patient needs more anaesthetic
C.why: A band that lifts or springs away has usually been positioned or assembled incorrectly in the retainer and needs reseating.

whyNot.0: The mix doesn't affect band fit before packing.
whyNot.2: Band fit has nothing to do with the curing light.
whyNot.3: Anaesthesia doesn't affect how a band seats.

C.q: While mixing glass ionomer, you realise the powder and liquid were measured in the wrong ratio. What should you do?
options: Add more liquid until it looks right
Use it, as the ratio doesn't matter
Discard it and remix correctly
Mix it for longer to compensate
C.why: An incorrect ratio weakens the material and changes its setting, so the mix is discarded and a fresh one made correctly.

whyNot.0: Adjusting by eye won't restore the correct properties.
whyNot.1: The manufacturer's ratio is essential for strength and setting.
whyNot.3: Extra mixing can't correct a wrong ratio and shortens working time.

reteach.title: Think of building a wall with a missing side
reteach.question: Imagine pouring concrete into a box that's lost one side. What would you need before you could pour?

blocks.body: Builders pouring concrete next to a gap put up formwork: a temporary wall that holds the shape until it sets. A matrix band is that formwork for a tooth that has lost its side wall in a Class II cavity. The wedge is the peg at the bottom that stops concrete leaking out under the board, which in a mouth would leave an overhang. Composite goes in like thin layers of render, each set with the light before the next, so the whole thing is solid and doesn't pull away as it shrinks.

blocks.text: Only proximal cavities need a matrix: Class II (back teeth) and Class III or IV (front teeth, usually with a clear strip).

explain.body: I: pits and fissures. II: proximal surfaces of premolars and molars. III: proximal surfaces of incisors and canines, angle intact. IV: as III but the incisal angle is involved. V: cervical third of the buccal/labial or lingual/palatal surface.

test.q: A small cavity is in the mesial surface of 12, with the incisal corner intact. Which class is it?
options: Class II
Class IV
Class III
Class I
test.why: A proximal cavity on an incisor without loss of the incisal angle is Class III.

whyNot.0: Class II is proximal on back teeth.
whyNot.1: Class IV would involve the incisal angle.
whyNot.3: Class I is pits and fissures.

explain.body: A band and retainer (or sectional matrix with ring) replaces the missing proximal wall; a clear strip is used for front teeth. The wedge adapts the band at the gum margin. Don't remove the band before the material has set.

test.q: What is the most likely result if the matrix band is removed before the material has set?
options: Loss of contour or fracture
The filling sets faster
Better contact with the next tooth
Less post-operative sensitivity
test.why: Unset material is weak, so removing the band too soon can fracture the filling or distort its shape and contact.

whyNot.1: Removing the band doesn't speed setting.
whyNot.2: Early removal usually spoils the contact point.
whyNot.3: It has no benefit for sensitivity.

explain.body: Mix capsules in the amalgamator, carry with the amalgam carrier, condense in increments, then carve and burnish. Place a lining under deep cavities to insulate the pulp. Never touch amalgam; waste goes in the amalgam container with mercury suppressant.

explain.caption: Deep cavities bring the filling close to the pulp, which is why a lining is placed under amalgam.

test.q: Why may a lining be placed under a deep amalgam restoration?
options: To make the amalgam set faster
To change the final colour of the filling
To bond the amalgam to enamel
To insulate the pulp from temperature
test.why: Amalgam conducts heat and cold, so a lining in a deep cavity insulates the pulp from thermal shocks.

whyNot.1: Linings are hidden underneath; they don't change the colour.
whyNot.2: Amalgam isn't bonded by a lining.

explain.body: Etch, rinse, controlled dry, bond, cure, then composite in increments, each cured. Saliva on an etched tooth ruins the bond, so tell the operator straight away. Replace contaminated tips.

test.q: During an anterior composite, you see saliva touch the etched tooth before bonding. What should you do?
options: Dry it quickly and say nothing
Apply extra bond to cover it
Inform the operator immediately
Add more composite to seal it
test.why: Saliva contamination spoils the etched surface, so the operator needs to know straight away to manage it (often by re-etching).

whyNot.0: Hiding contamination risks a failed filling.
whyNot.1: Extra bond won't fix a contaminated surface.
whyNot.3: Composite won't bond properly to a contaminated surface.
